questions.question: Can a commercial bank lend for construction of buildings used purely for government or semi-government offices, including municipal and panchayat offices?
questions.answer: No. A commercial bank must not finance such construction, but it may lend for activities that will be refinanced by institutions such as NABARD.
questions.evidence:
The bank shall not grant finance for the following:
(1) Construction of buildings meant purely for Government / Semi-Government offices, including Municipal and Panchayat offices. However, the bank may grant loans for activities, which will be refinanced by institutions like NABARD.

questions.question: For a commercially run housing project receiving government subsidies or capital contributions, how must a commercial bank determine the amount it may finance?
questions.answer: The bank must deduct the government subsidy or capital contribution and any other government resources proposed from the total project cost, and restrict its finance to the resulting amount.
questions.evidence: the bank finance shall be restricted to an amount arrived at after reducing from the total project cost the amount of subsidy / capital contribution receivable from the Government and any other resources proposed to be made available by the Government.

unanswerable.question: What is the maximum percentage of a government-subsidized housing project's total cost that a commercial bank may finance?
unanswerable.why: The paragraph requires subsidies, capital contributions, and other proposed government resources to be deducted from the total project cost, but it does not prescribe any percentage ceiling.

questions.question: What must a commercial bank do before it can launch a transactional banking facility, and where should it apply for approval?
questions.answer: It must obtain the Reserve Bank of India’s prior approval and satisfy the eligibility criteria. The application should be submitted to the Department of Regulation through the PRAVAAH portal, together with the appropriate authority’s approval and other supporting documents.
questions.evidence: 7.1 Banks shall require prior approval of the Reserve Bank for launching transactional banking facility. Subject to fulfilment of the eligibility criteria as enumerated below, banks may apply to the Department of Regulation, Reserve Bank of India (through the PRAVAAH portal) for launch of transactional banking facility, along with the approval of appropriate authority and other necessary supporting documents.

questions.question: After deciding to launch an additional digital banking channel, what must a commercial bank with an existing RBI approval submit, and by when?
questions.answer: It must send a GAICA Report certified by third-party CERT-In empanelled auditor(s), addressing the specific requirements of the new channel, to the Department of Regulation through the PRAVAAH portal. The report must be accompanied by the appropriate authority’s approval and submitted within thirty days from the decision to launch.
questions.evidence: Further, the GAICA Report, certified by (third party) CERT-In empanelled auditor(s), addressing the specific requirement for the new proposed channels shall be sent to the Department of Regulation, Reserve Bank of India (through the PRAVAAH portal) with the approval of appropriate authority within thirty days from the decision to launch the facility.

unanswerable.question: What is the maximum processing time for the Reserve Bank of India to approve a commercial bank’s transactional banking facility application?
unanswerable.why: The paragraph requires prior RBI approval and identifies the PRAVAAH application process, but it does not state any deadline or maximum processing period for the approval decision.

questions.question: A commercial bank wants to transfer a defaulted loan account with an outstanding of ₹30 lakh to another lender. What must the bank do on the wilful default front before the transfer, and is a two-stage committee compulsory?
questions.answer: The bank must internally conduct a comprehensive investigation from a wilful default perspective before transferring the loan, ensuring a thorough examination of wilful default aspects for that defaulted loan. A two-stage committee is not mandatory for this pre-transfer check.
questions.evidence: Before transferring a defaulted loan with outstanding of ₹25 lakh and above, irrespective of its classification as NPA, to other transferees, a bank shall internally conduct a comprehensive investigation from a wilful default perspective. This process need not necessarily involve a two-stage committee but should ensure a thorough examination of wilful default aspects for each defaulted loan.

questions.question: A commercial bank takes over a loan account in which wilful default was already observed by the transferor. How long must the new lender keep reporting the account as a wilful defaulter?
questions.answer: The transferee bank must continue reporting the account as a wilful defaulter until the balance remaining to be recovered in its account plus the amount written off by the transferor falls below ₹25 lakh (or such other threshold as RBI notifies from time to time), subject to Paragraph 13.
questions.evidence: A bank, which is a transferee in case of a loan in which wilful default has been observed, shall continue to report the account as a wilful defaulter until the balance remaining to be recovered in their account plus the amount written off by the transferor falls below the threshold of ₹25 lakh

unanswerable.question: Within how many days must a commercial bank complete the wilful default investigation before transferring a defaulted loan of ₹25 lakh or above?
unanswerable.why: The paragraph mandates a comprehensive wilful default investigation before transfer but does not state any time limit or deadline for completing it.

questions.question: If a commercial bank's borrower defaults, may the bank pursue the borrower's guarantor without first exhausting remedies against the borrower?
questions.answer: Yes. Once the principal debtor defaults in making payment or repayment, the bank may proceed against the guarantor without first exhausting remedies against the principal debtor.
questions.evidence: When a default happens in making payment / repayment by the principal debtor, a bank shall be able to proceed against the guarantor even without exhausting the remedies against the principal debtor.

questions.question: When a commercial bank is dealing with a wilfully defaulting company in a group, what should it do if guarantees furnished by other group companies for that unit are not honoured when the bank invokes them?
questions.answer: The bank should also consider those group companies for classification as wilful defaulters, using the mechanism set out in Paragraphs 5 and 6.
questions.evidence: In cases where guarantees furnished by the companies within the Group on behalf of the wilfully defaulting units are not honoured when invoked by the bank, such Group companies should also be considered for classification as willful defaulter by following the mechanism set out in Paragraphs 5 and 6.

unanswerable.question: What is the deadline for a commercial bank to classify a guarantor as a wilful defaulter after the guarantor refuses to comply with the bank's demand?
unanswerable.why: The paragraph requires the guarantor to be considered for classification through the mechanism in Paragraphs 5 and 6, but it states no time limit or deadline for completing that classification.

questions.question: As a compliance officer at a public sector bank, what must the Board do regarding discussions with management on the strength of the bank's internal control systems?
questions.answer: The Board must institutionalise discussions between management and the Board on the quality of the bank's internal control systems, and must pay specific attention to creating and sustaining a culture of control.
questions.evidence: A PSB shall institutionalise discussions between its management and the Board on quality of internal control systems. The Board shall specifically pay attention to creating and sustaining a culture of control.

questions.question: At a public sector bank, which areas must the Board keep under its oversight?
questions.answer: The Board must maintain oversight over the bank's risk management system, policy and strategy; its exposures to related entities, including details of lending to or investment in subsidiaries and the asset classification of such lending or investment; and conformity with corporate governance standards, such as the composition of committees, their role and functions, the periodicity of meetings and compliance with coverage and review functions.
questions.evidence: The Board shall maintain oversight on the following: (i) risk management system, policy and strategy followed by the PSB; (ii) exposures to related entities of the PSB, viz. details of lending to / investment in subsidiaries, the asset classification of such lending / investment, etc.; and (iii) conformity with corporate governance standards

unanswerable.question: How many times a year must the Board of a public sector bank meet with management to review the quality of the bank's internal control systems?
unanswerable.why: The paragraph requires the Board to institutionalise discussions on the quality of internal control systems and to sustain a culture of control, but it does not state any meeting frequency, number of reviews, or deadline for holding such discussions.

questions.question: As an NBFC, how often must we carry out a periodic review of the risk categorisation of our customer accounts?
questions.answer: At least once every six months, through a system of periodic review of risk categorisation of accounts.
questions.evidence: The NBFC shall put in place a system of periodic review of risk categorisation of accounts, with such periodicity being at least once in every six months

questions.question: What transaction monitoring does an NBFC have to apply to accounts of marketing firms, including MLM companies?
questions.answer: The NBFC must closely monitor transactions in accounts of marketing firms, with particular focus on accounts of Multi-level Marketing (MLM) companies.
questions.evidence: The NBFC shall closely monitor the transactions in accounts of marketing firms, especially accounts of Multi-level Marketing (MLM) companies.

unanswerable.question: What is the maximum period an NBFC has to complete enhanced due diligence on a customer account after it is classified as high risk?
unanswerable.why: The paragraph requires periodic review of risk categorisation at least once every six months and intensified monitoring of high-risk accounts, but it does not state any deadline for completing enhanced due diligence.

questions.question: As an NBFC, if a corporate customer is listed on an Indian stock exchange, do I still have to identify and verify its beneficial owners when opening an account?
questions.answer: No. Where the customer (or the owner of the controlling interest) is an entity listed on a stock exchange in India, an entity resident in a Central Government-notified jurisdiction and listed on a stock exchange there, or a subsidiary of such listed entities, the NBFC need not identify or verify the identity of any shareholder or beneficial owner.
questions.evidence: it is not necessary to identify and verify the identity of any shareholder or beneficial owner of such entities.

questions.question: For a trust or nominee account, what must an NBFC establish about the intermediaries and the persons they act for before opening the account?
questions.answer: The NBFC must determine whether the customer is acting on behalf of another person as trustee, nominee or other intermediary, and then obtain satisfactory evidence of the identity of the intermediaries and of the persons on whose behalf they act, together with details of the nature of the trust or other arrangement in place.
questions.evidence: the NBFC shall obtain satisfactory evidence of the identity of the intermediaries and of the persons on whose behalf they are acting, as well as details of the nature of the trust or other arrangements in place.

unanswerable.question: What minimum ownership percentage must an NBFC apply to decide that a natural person qualifies as a beneficial owner of a legal-person customer?
unanswerable.why: The paragraph requires an NBFC to identify and verify the beneficial owners of a legal-person customer, but it states no ownership threshold, percentage, or other numeric criterion for determining who counts as a beneficial owner.

questions.question: An NBFC offers monthly instalment (EMI) programmes on credit cards. Which regulatory directions govern these programmes, and do they fall within the scope of the Credit Facilities Directions?
questions.answer: EMI programmes on credit cards are governed specifically by the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025, and such transactions are not covered under the Credit Facilities Directions.
questions.evidence: EMI programmes on Credit Card are governed specifically by the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025. Such transactions shall not be covered under these Directions.

questions.question: An NBFC enters into a digital lending arrangement with its loan service provider (LSP) in line with the Digital Lending chapter. How is such an arrangement treated for synthetic securitisation and loan participation purposes?
questions.answer: Where the NBFC-LSP digital lending arrangement conforms to the instructions in the Digital Lending chapter, it is neither treated as synthetic securitisation under the Securitisation Transactions Directions, 2025 nor does it attract the provisions on loan participation under the Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk Directions, 2025.
questions.evidence: DLG arrangements entered between an NBFC and their LSP conforming to the instructions laid down in this Chapter shall neither be treated as “synthetic securitisation” as defined under the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Securitisation Transactions) Directions, 2025, nor attract the provisions of ‘loan participation’

unanswerable.question: What is the maximum loan-to-value ratio and maximum tenure an NBFC may offer when lending against gold jewellery, ornaments and coins as collateral?
unanswerable.why: The paragraph only gives the background and rationale for restricting lending against primary gold and permitting lending against gold jewellery, ornaments and coins; it states no loan-to-value ratio, loan amount cap, or tenure for such lending against gold or silver collateral.

questions.question: For digital loans offered by an NBFC, what is the shortest cooling-off period the lender must provide, and who determines the actual period?
questions.answer: The NBFC determines the cooling-off period under its credit policy, but the period cannot be less than one day.
questions.evidence: The cooling off period shall be determined by the NBFC in terms of their credit policy, subject to the period so determined not being less than one day.

questions.question: If a customer exits an NBFC digital loan during the cooling-off period, can the lender charge a processing fee?
questions.answer: Yes. The NBFC may retain a reasonable one-time processing fee, provided it is disclosed to the customer upfront in the KFS.
questions.evidence: An NBFC may retain a reasonable one-time processing fee, if the customer exits the loan during the cooling-off period. This, if applicable, shall be disclosed to the customer upfront in KFS.

unanswerable.question: What is the maximum cooling-off period that an NBFC may set for a digital loan?
unanswerable.why: The paragraph requires the NBFC-determined cooling-off period to be at least one day, but it does not state any maximum period.

questions.question: As an NBFC that lends against gold and silver, what must we do to check the collateral borrowers pledge, and what record-keeping does this require?
questions.answer: The NBFC must carry out periodic surprise verification of the gold and silver collateral pledged with it as part of internal audit, and must maintain a record of those verifications.
questions.evidence: As part of internal audit, an NBFC shall carry out periodic surprise verification of the gold and silver collateral pledged with it and shall maintain a record thereof.

questions.question: For an NBFC's gold or silver-backed loans, what needs to be included in the loan agreement about borrower consent for checking the collateral, and when must the borrower be informed?
questions.answer: The loan agreement must contain a clause obtaining the borrower's consent to surprise verification, including assay of the pledged eligible collateral even in the borrower's absence during the loan tenure. This must be specifically communicated to the borrower at the time the loan is sanctioned.
questions.evidence: A clause in the loan agreement shall be included for obtaining consent of the borrower(s) to carry out surprise verification including assay of the pledged eligible collateral even in their absence during the tenor of the loan. This aspect shall be specifically communicated to the borrower at the time of sanctioning the loan.

unanswerable.question: How often must an NBFC conduct surprise verification of the gold and silver collateral pledged with it — for example, how many times per year or at what interval?
unanswerable.why: The paragraph requires only that surprise verification be 'periodic' and does not state any frequency, number of verifications, or time interval.

questions.question: As an NBFC, are the penal measures in Paragraphs 35 and 36 still applicable to a business enterprise after its resolution plan under the IBC has been implemented?
questions.answer: No. Once the resolution plan under the IBC or the aforesaid resolution framework has been implemented, those penal measures are no longer applicable to the entity or business enterprise.
questions.evidence: The penal measures as detailed in Paragraphs 35 and 36 shall not be applicable to entities / business enterprises after implementation of the Resolution Plan under Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) or aforesaid resolution framework.

questions.question: Can an NBFC rely on the same exclusion from the Paragraphs 35 and 36 penal measures when a resolution plan is implemented under the rulebook's other resolution framework rather than under the IBC?
questions.answer: Yes. The exclusion applies after implementation of a resolution plan under either the IBC or the aforesaid resolution framework.
questions.evidence: The penal measures as detailed in Paragraphs 35 and 36 shall not be applicable to entities / business enterprises after implementation of the Resolution Plan under Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) or aforesaid resolution framework.

unanswerable.question: How many days after implementation of an IBC resolution plan does an NBFC have before it must discontinue applying the penal measures in Paragraphs 35 and 36?
unanswerable.why: Paragraph 38 specifies no number of days, grace period, or other deadline; the exclusion takes effect after implementation of the resolution plan.

questions.question: For an NBFC operating a peer-to-peer lending platform, what must the RBI find about its promoters, directors, and management when considering registration?
questions.answer: The promoters and directors must be fit and proper, and the management’s general character must not be prejudicial to the public interest. The grant of the Certificate of Registration must also serve the public interest.

questions.question: May the RBI impose additional conditions for registering an NBFC peer-to-peer lending platform beyond the standard eligibility requirements?
questions.answer: Yes. The RBI may specify any additional condition it considers necessary to ensure that the commencement or continuation of the business in India will not be prejudicial to the public interest.
questions.evidence: (9) Any other condition as may be specified by the Reserve Bank, fulfillment of which, in the opinion of the Reserve Bank, is necessary to ensure that the commencement of or carrying on the business in India shall not be prejudicial to the public interest.

unanswerable.question: What minimum net worth or paid-up capital must an NBFC peer-to-peer lending platform have to qualify for registration with the RBI?
unanswerable.why: The paragraph requires an adequate capital structure but does not state any minimum capital amount or other numerical threshold.
